# FIT5145 Assignment 1

## Data-Driven Pacing Corridors for HYROX Pro Division Athletes

Name: Lim Excelyynx   
Student ID: 34476245

### **1.0 Introduction**

HYROX is one of the fastest-growing participation sports globally: eight 1 km runs alternate with eight functional stations, and participation rose from 570,000 athletes in the 2024/25 season to 1.5 million in 2025/26 (SportsPro, 2026). Mid-race pacing decisions are currently made with little objective guidance, so this project asks whether information available immediately after Station 4 — roughly the halfway point — can predict how much each athlete will slow across the remaining runs, rather than merely benchmark a completed race.

The analytical population is operationally defined as individual HYROX Pro division finishers in the 2025/26 (Season 8) results with valid run and station split times; the Pro division is verifiable through the Division field, so results are not claimed for groups the dataset cannot identify (such as first-time racers). One observation represents one athlete-race across all eight runs and stations.   
   
The goals are to describe how running pace varies across the race, to test whether early station performance adds predictive information beyond early running splits alone (via an ablation), and to produce a calibrated uncertainty corridor for later running time that coaches can interpret.

### **2.0 Related Work**

#### 2.1 Existing projects

Brandt et al. (2025) characterised the physiological demands of HYROX in a simulated race with 11 recreational athletes, using Wilcoxon tests and Spearman correlations to link running and station performance. This supports examining runs and stations together, but describes a single race and does not test checkpoint-based prediction of subsequent slowdown.

Miyazaki et al. (2025) predicted severe late-race slowing ("hitting the wall") from first-half wearable biomechanics, reaching 73.9% accuracy on a held-out test subset of 134 marathon runners. Early-warning prediction is therefore not new, but their approach requires inertial sensors, applies a binary threshold (a pace reduction above 25%) that excludes intermediate slowing, and does not estimate a continuous slowdown magnitude.

On the applied side, HyroxDataLab (2026) offers segment percentiles and goal-time pacing tools, while HyroxVault's (2026) race-time calculator predicts finish times from fitness inputs and explicitly acknowledges that it "does not know how badly you'll fade in the back half". None of the reviewed tools demonstrates a validated forecast from the athlete's own unfolding race at Station 4; this is a bounded gap in the reviewed work, not a claim that no comparable system exists.

#### 2.2 Novelty

The proposed contribution is a split-only, mid-race checkpoint forecast built on one testable question: does early decline — slowdown across Runs 1–4 plus early station-relative performance — carry information about late-race collapse (Runs 5–8) beyond early running pace alone? Two design choices make this measurable: each station time is normalised against its own training-set distribution, because raw durations of different exercises cannot express a common fatigue trajectory, and interaction features pair each station-relative time with the change in the following run using only information observable by Run 4. An ablation then compares running-only and run-plus-station models with everything else held constant, so any information gain is measured through test-error differences and the association between early decline and later slowdown, not asserted.

This extends the reviewed work in three concrete ways: it forecasts a continuous slowdown magnitude with an uncertainty corridor rather than a binary outcome, and without specialist sensors (Miyazaki et al., 2025); it updates the forecast mid-race from the athlete's own splits rather than returning a static estimate that admits back-half fading is unmodelled (HyroxVault, 2026); and it validates on held-out events rather than describing one simulated race (Brandt et al., 2025). If station features add no measurable value, the ablation will show it — a null result is an informative finding.

#### 2.3 Importance

The stakes are documented. An international survey of 418 HYROX athletes found that 49.8% reported at least one injury within 12 months (an exposure-adjusted lower bound of 1.65 injuries per 1,000 training hours), most commonly at the knee (20.8%) and tendon tissue (41.6%) (Ketzer et al., 2026); in a sport where entries and tickets generate 55–65% of revenue (SportsPro, 2026), injuries affect participants and the commercial model alike. In a simulated race, peak heart rate, lactate and perceived exertion all occurred at the final station (Brandt et al., 2025), and technique breakdown of 25–35% under fatigue at heavy loaded stations is linked to injury risk (Bauerfeind, n.d.). No study yet connects pacing collapse directly to injury, but the evidence establishes substantial strain concentrated in the race's back half — exactly where an early-warning signal would act.

For athletes, an accessible forecast could set realistic expectations and give coaches an objective basis for pacing discussions; for gyms, replaying race trajectories could make debriefs more specific and reduce manual analysis. A free basic report would widen access beyond athletes who purchase specialist sensors. Benefits would be evaluated through prediction error, coach-reported usefulness and analysis time saved; improved retention, injury prevention and faster finishes remain unproven and are not claimed. Alerts must avoid false reassurance or pressure to maintain an unsafe pace.

### **3.0 Business Model**

#### 3.1 Data Business Model

The data business model is analytics-as-a-service: historical public race results are refined into a derived data product — calibrated pacing forecasts — and sold by subscription, rather than reselling raw athlete records. The value chain runs from acquisition (scraped or licensed results) and curation (cleaning, normalisation, quality auditing) to modelling (the checkpoint forecast) and delivery (a coach-facing report or dashboard). The primary stakeholders are HYROX, which can differentiate its race experience and activate its timing data; coaches and affiliated gyms, the prospective subscribers, who gain objective pacing evidence instead of manual spreadsheet analysis; and athletes, the beneficiaries, who receive interpreted, uncertainty-aware guidance. Revenue would fund data maintenance, validation and dashboard support; demand and willingness to pay require testing.

Data acquisition starts with the official results published on the HYROX all-time ranking site, extracted to CSV by a Python scraper adapted from imterence's open-source repository (HYROX, 2026; imterence, 2025). The raw records include name, city, age group, all workout split times, total time and ranking; governance of this reused public data is discussed in Section 5.

Deployment is staged. Stage 1, the current prototype, replays historical races in R with everything after Station 4 hidden, proving feasibility and estimating accuracy. Stage 2, the near-term product, delivers post-race reports generated from the official results feed, making the service saleable without live infrastructure. Stage 3, the future service, would receive licensed timestamped splits during a race (or consented manual input), compute features in near real time and return a forecast corridor to the coach dashboard. Public results access does not prove live-feed availability: race-day use requires latency testing, written permission and prospective validation, none of which the prototype claims.

#### 3.2 Level of Analytics

The project spans three analytical levels. Descriptive analytics summarises run trajectories, station-relative distributions and slowdown by sex and event. Predictive analytics compares a training-median slowdown baseline, a running-only linear regression and a run-plus-station regression, with a random forest as an optional nonlinear comparator. The forecast corridor is prescriptive in intent — it supports hold-or-adjust pacing decisions — but remains decision support, because causal effects of pacing changes are not estimated.

Evaluation holds out whole events, removes training records of identifiable test athletes and fits preprocessing on training data only. Models are reported on mean absolute error in slowdown percentage points, absolute later-running-time error and prediction-interval coverage. Final time, finishing rank and later splits cannot be predictors. 

#### 3.3 Challenges

Missing or misassigned splits, penalties, transition timing and venue layouts can distort apparent slowing: audit records, document exclusions and test sensitivity to anomalous runs. Missing outcomes cannot be imputed and are excluded. Because early and late times are proportions of the same race, shared denominators can inflate apparent associations, so predictions of absolute later running time are evaluated alongside slowdown.

### **4.0 Characterising and Analysing Data**

#### 4.1 Potential Data Source, Characteristics (4V), Platforms and Tools

The first option is the official HYROX Season 8 results, extracted to local CSV with an adapted Python scraper based on imterence's open-source repository (HYROX, 2026; imterence, 2025). 

1) Volume: the two datasets — hyrox\_season8\_male\_pro.csv (4,746 KB; 12,400 rows) and hyrox\_season8\_female\_pro.csv (4,789 KB; 12,500 rows) — hold rank, name, age group, division, total and roxzone times, eight run splits, eight station splits and an athlete-detail URL. This volume is small enough for in-memory analysis on a single laptop in RStudio.  
2) Variety: modest — tabular identifiers, categorical fields and colon-formatted time strings (e.g., 00:02:42).  
3) Velocity: batch updates after each race, not a verified live stream.  
4) Veracity: requires substantial checking — City is missing for every row, and rows with missing splits must be excluded before modelling.

The second option is JGug's Kaggle HYROX results, described as covering Seasons 4–6 with event identifiers and division metadata (JGug, 2024). 

1) Volume: hyrox\_results.csv (25.31 MB; 92,374 rows) exceeds option one in volume, but records only overall total, roxzone, work and run times — no individual run or station split times.  
2) Variety: adds event and division metadata.  
3) Velocity: a periodic historical publication, not a live stream.  
4) Veracity: depends on coverage, missing splits, division harmonisation and whether the download actually supplies all eight run splits. It is useful for historical validation if these checks pass, but older seasons can differ from Season 8 and the Kaggle listing's season description and file preview are not fully consistent, so coverage must be confirmed locally before pooling.

The third option is a third-party HYROX Result API exposing versioned JSON event, athlete and split endpoints (HYROX Result API, 2025).

1) Volume: scales across events.  
2) Variety: nested JSON and event metadata.  
3) Velocity: depends on provider updates rather than a guaranteed Station-4 live feed.  
4) Veracity: requires checking split completeness, latency and provider provenance.

The API's public sandbox shows sample responses rather than real-time checkpoint delivery, so live use would require a paid plan and a permission check. For the current analysis, R, RStudio and the tidyverse (with lubridate and hms for time parsing) suffice, and a Kaggle download provides an equivalent offline fallback. If the project expands — live streams, multi-season history (which would also let a debut/first-time cohort be identified from prior-season records) or a larger event catalogue — a scheduled ingestion pipeline into a managed relational or cloud store with automated schema and quality tests would replace repeated CSV downloads, and a paid API subscription would become preferable to maintaining a scraper, subject to cost, licensing and permission checks.

#### 4.2 Data Analysis Approach

The unit of analysis is one athlete-race: a verified HYROX Pro division entry with valid splits, sex recorded from its source file, and split strings parsed into time format; rows missing the checkpoint or outcome are excluded rather than imputed. The process runs in three stages: (1) clean and parse; (2) profile data quality and describe pacing degradation by sex; and (3) predict later running with quantified uncertainty and report.

Descriptive analysis defines early running time as the mean of Runs 1–4 and later running time as the mean of Runs 5–8, with slowdown defined as 100 × (later − early) / early; negative values indicate a faster second half. Distributions and trajectories are described by sex using quartiles and the coefficient of variation, without treating station time as a direct physiological measure of fatigue.

Predictive analysis compares a baseline — each division's training-median slowdown applied to the athlete's early mean — against a linear model of later mean on early mean with division-specific intercepts and slopes, using an 80/20 train-test split. Event-held-out evaluation is impossible because event identity is missing, so a random row split is used and generalisation is claimed only to similar-season Pro fields. Spearman rank correlation checks the early–later association, as it is robust to the skew and outliers typical of split times. Models are compared on test mean absolute error in seconds and as a percentage; the prediction corridor is built from training residual quantiles, with empirical coverage and width reported on the untouched test set by division. Because early and late means derive from the same race, absolute later-time error is evaluated alongside percentage slowdown. The expected outcome is an auditable mid-race forecast with a calibrated corridor; poor coverage would restrict the application to post-race analysis rather than justify a race-day claim.
